text:
Citation:

Miller v.
Canadian Broadcasting Corp. et al

Date:

20030217

2003 BCSC 258

Docket:

SO22590

Registry:  Vancouver

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF
BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

JANICE MILLER

PLAINTIFF

AND:

CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION

and MARGO HARPER

DEFENDANTS

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE MADAM JUSTICE SATANOVE

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

D.H.
Christie

Counsel for the Defendants:

R.R.
Sugden, Q.C.

and
P.F. Lewis

Date and Place of Hearing:

January
13, 14 and 22, 2003

Vancouver, BC

[
1
]

On November 19, 1996, the defendant Canadian
Broadcasting Corporation (the “CBC”) aired a 17 minute program about Canada’s hate movement (the “Broadcast”).
It focused on two individuals:  Terry Long, a previous Canadian leader of the
Aryan Nations organization; and Charles Scott, a self-proclaimed Christian
preacher.

[
2
]

The plaintiff has been married to Terry Long
since l970.  The CBC Broadcast referred to her four times:

1.   .
. . home on 20th Avenue in
Creston was on the market.  It’s owner, an R.C.M.P. member, got a good offer
from a pharmacist named Janice Lynn Miller, Terry Long’s wife, using her maiden
name.  . . . That fall, the Long children, Becky and Cody, started high school
in Creston.

2.   In
1986 at the annual Aryan Nations Congress in Hayden
Lake, Idaho, Terry Long was acclaimed Canada’s High Aryan Warrior Priest.
The
Longs dressed their kids up in pint sized Klan uniforms for the celebratory
cross burning.
(my emphasis)

3.   .
. . A case that haunts Terry Long to this day:  the 1990 beating and blinding
of retired Edmonton radio
reporter, Keith Rutherford . . . he pressed on with the civil suite for 2.5
million dollars.  Named in the suit are Terry and Janice Long and the skin
heads who blinded him.

4.   .
. . The Longs have been living in the valley for three and a half years.

[
3
]

The plaintiff commenced a defamation action on August 12, 1998 allegeging that the statement set
out in bold print above was false and defamatory.  She pleaded in her statement
of claim, inter alia, that:

7. …the allegation of causing their children to
be dressed in pint-sized Klan uniforms was false and malicious and defamatory
…the aforesaid statement by implication associated the plaintiff with the other
public demonstrations and racist’s political beliefs of her husband depicted in
the broadcast.

8. The truth was, and remains, that the
plaintiff was not associated with public activities of her husband and did not
dress her children in pint-sized Klan outfits or in any way cause them to
participate in Ku Klux Klan activities.

[
4
]

The defendants pleaded, inter alia,
justification of a lesser defamatory meaning, or alternatively, substantial
justification:

7.   Alternatively,
the defendants say that, insofar as the plaintiff is concerned, the words
complained of, in the context of the Broadcast as a whole, meant and would have
been understood by the ordinary, reasonable viewer to mean that, with her
husband, she exposed her children to an expression of racist ideology to which
she was sympathetic.  This was true in substance and in fact.

…

8.   In
the alternative, in their context, the words complained of are substantially
true.  The words complained of contain the following elements, expressly or by
clear implication:

a.   Terry Long was acclaimed leader of Canada’s Aryan Nations Organization in 1986 at the annual Aryan Nations
Congress in Hayden Lake, Idaho;

b.   The plaintiff was married to Terry Long;

c.   There was a cross burning on this occasion;

d.   The plaintiff was present at the cross burning;

e.   The plaintiff and her husband took their children to the cross
burning;

f.   For this occasion Terry Long and the plaintiff dressed their
children in pint sized Klan uniforms.

The assertions contained in sub-paragraph a, b,
c, d, and e are true and, accordingly, even if it is found that the assertion
contained in sub-paragraph f is untrue, the fact is that the words complained
of are substantially true and no liability should be found.

[
5
]

The defendants applied before this court for a
summary judgment on the issues of justification of a lesser meaning, or
substantial justification.  The plaintiff opposed the matter proceeding by way
of Rule 18A and alternatively, opposed dismissal of the plaintiff’s claim on
these issues.

ISSUES

I.  Is the
matter suitable for disposition by rule 18A?

II.  What is the sting of the libel?

III. Has it been justified, or
substantially justified on the evidence adduced to date?

Rule 18A

[
6
]

The plaintiff submitted the case should proceed
to trial for 10 days on its commencement date of May 5, 2003.  Her counsel
submitted there was a vast difference between what the plaintiff has admitted
on her examination for discovery and what has been alleged by the defendants.
He said the defendants have not made out their defences and the court requires viva
voce testimony and expert evidence before it can fairly judge the matter.

[
7
]

In my view these issues are appropriate for
disposition by Rule 18A.  For some reason the plaintiff chose to adduce no
evidence of her own.  Mr. Christie’s position on her behalf was tantamount to
an insufficient evidence motion at trial.  He made no effort to adduce proper
evidence to contradict, clarify or supplement the body of evidence before me,
other than an attempt to use parts of the defendants examination for discovery
of the plaintiff which had not been read in by the defendants, and which I
would not allow him to do pursuant to Rule 40(27).

[
8
]

There are no issues of credibility or
conflicting evidence for me to decide.  The only question is whether it would
be unjust to give judgment.  I must take into account whether there is
sufficient evidence for me to adjudicate upon, the amount involved, the
complexity of the matter, its urgency, any prejudice likely to arise by reason
of delay, the costs of proceeding to a conventional trial in relation to the
amount involved, the course of the proceedings and any other matters which
arise for consideration on this question.  (
Inspiration Management Ltd.,
et al, v.
McDermid St.
Lawrence Ltd.
(1989),
1989 CanLII 229 (BC CA)
, 36 B.C.L.R.
2d 202 (B.C.C.A.)).

[
9
]

I have answered the question in the affirmative,
that is, I am able to and should give judgment in accordance with Rule 18A.
Examinations for discovery have concluded and there is ample evidence from the
plaintiff’s own admissions for me to decide the issues.  The amount of damages
sought, although not liquidated, are not likely high because the plaintiff’s
complaints of losing her employment and being isolated in the community arose
before the Broadcast was aired.  The Broadcast was released in 1996, yet the
plaintiff took no steps until 1998 and it is now over 6 years since this
statement was made.  A ten day trial would involve both parties in unnecessary
expense with very little to be gained at the end of the day.

The Sting of the Libel

[
10
]

In her pleadings, the plaintiff states that the sting of the libel
is that she is being associated with the other public demonstrations and racist
political beliefs of her husband depicted in the Broadcast.

[
11
]

On her examination for discovery the plaintiff states that she was
bothered because the statement insinuated that her children were Ku Klux Klan
members and that she had attended a Ku Klux Klan meeting, which was all
untrue.

[
12
]

On the application before me, counsel submitted that the sting of
the libel was its suggestion that the plaintiff forcibly indoctrinated her
children in racist ideology and had them participate in cross burnings.

[
13
]

In light of the discrepancy amongst the plaintiff’s pleadings,
evidence and submissions, it is somewhat difficult to grasp what she maintains is
the sting of the libel.  However, in order to successfully make out their
defences in paragraphs 7 and 8, the defendants do not have to accept any of the
plaintiff’s alleged defamatory meanings of the impugned statement.

A series of decisions commencing in 1986
established that a defendant is permitted to plead any defamatory meaning of
the words in question which those words are capable of bearing for the purpose
of pleading and proving that in such meaning the words are true or fair comment.

(
Pizza Pizza Ltd. v. Toronto Star
Newspapers Ltd.
(1998),
1998 CanLII 18866 (ON CA)
, 167 D.L.R. (4th) 748 at 754 Ont. Div. Ct.).

***********

…the defendant is entitled to look at the whole
publication in order to aver that in their context the words bear a meaning
different to that alleged by the plaintiff.  The defendant is entitled to plead
that in that meaning the words are true . . .

(
Polly Peck Holdings v. Trelford,
[1986]
2 All E.R. 84 at 102 (C.A.)
).

[
14
]

The only limitation on this right to plead and prove justification
of a lesser defamatory meaning is that a defendant must not act oppressively.
The plaintiff in the case at bar makes no complaint of oppression, nor does she
challenge the right of the defendants to plead a different meaning, but says
the defendants cannot succeed on the evidence in establishing the different
meaning they are alleging.

[
15
]

The plaintiff submits that the statement implies much more than
merely exposing children to other beliefs.  This would not be condemned by
right thinking people and therefore is not defamatory.  Children are exposed to
extremist views on television and merely observing a cross burning as a
bystander is no different.  Her counsel submitted that it is the element of
participation or indoctrination which makes the statement offensive and
defamatory.

[
16
]

I do not agree with this submission of the plaintiff.  For the
purposes of this application, however, it is not necessary, nor indeed
desirable, to analyze the effect of the statement too closely.  Lord Reid, in
Rubber
Improvement Ltd. v. Daily Telegraph Ltd.,
[1964] A.C. 234 at 258 (H.L.)

said this:

There is no doubt that in actions for libel the
question is what the words would convey to an ordinary man:  it is not one of
construction in the legal sense.  The ordinary man does not live in an ivory
tower and he is not inhibited by a knowledge of the rules of construction.  So
he can and does read between the lines in the light of his general knowledge
and experience of worldly affairs…

What the ordinary man would infer without
special knowledge has generally been called the natural and ordinary meaning of
the words.  But that expression is rather misleading in that it conceals the
fact that there are two elements in it.  Sometimes it is not necessary to go
beyond the words themselves as where the plaintiff has been called a thief or a
murderer.  But more often the sting is not so much in the words themselves as
in what the ordinary man will infer from them and that is also regarded as part
of their natural and ordinary meaning.

[
17
]

It is for the trier of fact, in this case myself, to decide what
natural and ordinary meaning the words bear, including what innuendo can be reasonably
inferred.  I am not bound by either the interpretation of the plaintiff or the
defendants.  (
Lucas – Box v. News Group Newspapers Ltd.,
[1986] l
All E.R. 177 (C.A.)).

[
18
]

I have reviewed the statement in the context of the Broadcast as a
whole (
Polly Peck,
supra)
.
The other references to
the plaintiff and the Long children in the Broadcast lead me to conclude that
the sting of the libel is not so mild as mere “exposure to racist beliefs”, nor
so powerful as “forcible indoctrination”.  In my view the defamatory aspect of
the statement is that it implies that Terry Long, notorious racist, has
involved his wife and children in his expression of racist ideology and that it
is a family affair.  In reaching this conclusion, I am relying on the other
references to the plaintiff which I enumerated earlier and also the references
to the Long children made throughout the tape.  The statement that the Longs
dressed their kids in pint sized Klan uniforms is just another insinuation that
it is a family affair, although this statement of how they were dressed is not
literally true.

[
19
]

Therefore, the question from the defendants’ perspective should be
whether it is true that the plaintiff has been involved in this expression of racist
ideals and whether she has involved her children in forms of that expression.

Justification

[
20
]

The plaintiff submits that because she refused to answer questions
on examination for discovery as to what her private beliefs are, there is no
evidence to justify the defamation.  However, I have found the sting of the libel
to be in her “involvement” with her husband’s ideology and her involvement of
their children with this ideology.

[
21
]

In my view, there is ample evidence before me to prove, on a balance
of probabilities, that the plaintiff and her children were involved with Mr.
Long’s racist beliefs and activities.

[
22
]

The following summary is a paraphrasing of answers given by the
plaintiff on her examination for discovery:

1.   Terry Long was the Alberta Aryan Nations leader in 1984.  He
was a Canadian leader of Aryan Nations until 1991.

2.   She never publicly opposed anything Terry Long said or did.

3.   She was proud of him for attaining certain positions in the
right wing movement.

4.   These are some of the tenets of the Aryan Nation:

a)   White
people should live in their own segregated areas;

b)   Jewish
people are the children of Satan;

c)   Jewish
people are less than human;

d)   Jewish
people should be exterminated (Armageddon);

e)   Jews
are responsible for all major problems in society.

5.   She has heard these tenets expressed in speeches and audio
tapes many times over the years.

6.   She has listened to tapes of sermons and speeches for her own
learning and interest.

7.   She attended sermons at the Aryan Nation’s congresses at Hayden Lake.  She
spent more time with the women and children.  They had a lot of children’s
activities that she was involved in.

8.   The Ku Klux Klan were one of the groups who attended Hayden Lake.  She heard them speak.

9.   Her
purpose in attending the gatherings at Hayden Lake was to meet people and hear ideas.

10.  The
congress was exclusively for whites and non-Jews.

11.  She
attended approximately 5 or 6 of these Hayden Lake annual gatherings.  There was a cross lighting at each of
them.  The first one was in 1984.  She went with her husband and her three
children.  She helped cook and helped with the children’s activities.  The
children were taught “religion” by somebody.

12.  The
children stood alongside her at the cross lighting.  So did reporters.  There
were people in Ku Klux Klan uniforms with hoods on.  The sermon explained to
them what these people were, including references to whites being the supreme
race, etc.

13.  She,
her husband and three children attended the Congress in 1986.  They were there
for 4 or 5 days.  Her husband became leader of the Canadian Aryan Nations.  She
knew what to expect in terms of the events of the week-end.  They attended the
cross lighting again, with people in Ku Klux Klan robes and hoods.  Her husband
was in the center of the circle when he was named Canadian leader.

14.  The
1986 congress was called to discuss the establishment of a white only territorial
imperative.  Her husband wanted this established.

15.  There
were people at Hayden Lake in Nazi style uniforms in 1986.  She saw a Nazi style salute on
more than one occasion.  Her children have seen their father wearing an Aryan
Nations badge.  They had already seen it at Hayden Lake.

16.  She also attended similar congresses at Hayden Lake with
her husband and children in 1987, 1988, 1989 and 1990.

17.  She
says after the children had been to Hayden Lake there was no need to explain what the place was about on
future occasions.

18.  She
didn’t have a view, nor was she concerned at that time as to whether a cross
lighting with people robed in Ku Klux Klan garb was a good place for a young
child to be at.

19.  She
took no steps to disassociate herself with the beliefs expressed at the
conferences.

20.  She
and her husband enrolled their two daughters in the Living
Faith Bible School in Caroline, Alberta.  Their daughter took the book,
The Hoax of the 20th
Century
, to the school.  The school wanted her to take the book home.  The
Plaintiff and her husband took their daughters out of that school because of
the position the school had taken with respect to that book.

21.  The
book questioned the Holocaust, etc.  She was concerned because the school was
not open to the alternative view point expressed in that book.

22.  She
prepared and recorded a telephone message for use by the Canadian Liberty Net
on its messages system.

23.  In
it she chose to describe Canada
as the Soviet Peoples Republic of Canada because there was a large lack of
freedom in this country.  She referred to “Esau/Edomites” and admitted that this
was a reference to Jewish people.  She admitted that she regarded the Jewish
people as being in control in this country and in control of society in the
western world.  She admitted that “Esau/Edomites” was a critical reference to
the Jewish people by reason of their blood and birth.

24.  She
composed the telephone message herself, without assistance.

[
23
]

In light of this uncontradicted evidence which came from the
plaintiff’s own mouth, I find the sting of the libel to be justified, or
substantially true.

SUBSTANTIALLY TRUE

[
24
]

I find that sub-paragraph (a) through (e) of paragraph 8 of the
statement of defence has been made out by the examination for discovery
evidence above.  I agree with the defendants that the information that the
children were dressed in a way consistent with the event is immaterial.  Once
again, I believe what the viewer takes away from the Broadcast is that the
Longs were there as a family, fully supporting Terry Long as he was powerfully
proclaimed a racist leader, all of which would shock the sensibilities of the
ordinary, reasonable person.  As this was proven to be true, the detail of how
the children were dressed is irrelevant.

CONCLUSION

[
25
]

The defendant has succeeded in justifying the defamatory statement,
both in fact and at law, and I dismiss the plaintiff’s claim with costs.

“D.A. Satanove, J.”

The Honourable Madam Justice D.A. Satanove
